items.text: 米国流通視察はなぜ時代遅れなのか？ 日本からの米国流通視察では、いまだに店舗を歩き、棚を眺め、写真を撮って終わる研修が少なくない。 しかし、売場だけを見ても、米国小売業の本当の競争力は理解できない時代になった。 ウォルマートを訪れても、アプリを操作せず、ネットスーパーで注文せず、商品の受け取りも体験しない。それでは小売業の最も重要なリアルな変化を見落としてしまう。 同じ問題は、売場写真を中心... このコンテンツは FASHIONSNAP が配信しています。

Finding her character between moments of routine, everyday action, and dance, Khalid – along with lead actor Toni O’Rourke and cinematographer Joel Honeywell – explore the beauty in the mundane and the simple actions that give meaning to ‘in-between’ spaces. The approach was one of improvisation. It's often in the in-between moments, just before or after something happens, that I find things most alive on-screen. They are where a character truly reveals themselves to an audience, and to themselves. Inspired by durational cinema and the presence of routine on-screen, Khalid considers how films that demand time and active participation from their audience initiate a powerful exchange between viewer and character – with these ‘in-between’ moments as a place where a character truly reveals themselves to an audience, and to themselves.

items.text: ​Can You Hear This? Sound-driven creative studio Father investigates transformation from the space between the natural and the analog for the short film Can You Hear This? , asking what a sound becomes once it stops being raw. We set up a mobile studio within Dungeness itself where we spent several days creating music together, inspired by the unique environment which surrounded us. We went to listen, document, and find a state of presence. Capturing the landscapes and soundscapes of Dungeness on England’s Kent coast, the team gathered field recordings by using hydrophones and contact mics on stone, bark, and other materials that don't make sounds, taking the recordings apart and building them into something else entirely. Studying the intersection between raw sounds and process, Can You Hear This? celebrates the act of listening together and the creative possibilities that emerge from it, inspired by the rugged nature of this unique coastal environment.

items.text: Jacolby Satterwhite - A Metta Prayer New York-based artist Jacolby Satterwhite’s A Metta Prayer (2023) is a multimedia, site-specific installation that was projected onto the walls of the Great Hall at the Metropolitan Museum of Art (The Met) in Manhattan. In an excerpt from the 21-minute, six-channel video, enter a virtual universe that brings together music, choreography, and animation in ecstatic scenes that celebrate hope, joy, and liberation. Satterwhite’s time-based piece echoes the grammar of endless-runner video games but eschews the gratuitous violence and exploitation that is common to this genre. Channeling the Buddhist Metta prayer of loving-kindness, the artist creates a mantra of his own, inspired by queer freedom of existence and expression. A Metta Prayer features Satterwhite collaborators including musicians Solange Knowles, Kelsey Lu and Moses Sumney, as well as drag artist Laveau Contraire, queer wrestling collective Choke Hole, and dance artist O'Shae Sibley. Over the last few years, Satterwhite has been fighting a public battle with complications due to cancer, and he is the inaugural recipient of the newly established Artists Living with Cancer Grant from the Rema Hort Mann Fund .

items.text: ​Limber Up: Arena en el Tiempo The oldest horse races in Spain, held for nearly two centuries, the Sanlúcar Horse Races – or, the Carreras de Caballos de Sanlúcar de Barrameda – are an annual tradition that lasts for just a few minutes, yet has endured for generations. Taking over a stretch of coastline at sunset each August, the beach spectacle is charged with emotion, both for those who race and those who watch from the sidelines – consistent since its beginnings as a race between merchants, competing to be first to the fishing boats for the best catch. I wanted to pay tribute to this tradition from within, where the intensity of each moment becomes part of a story that is still alive. Capturing the legendary Sanlúcar Horse Races through the jockey’s perspective, director Sergio Abuja translates the feeling and emotion of the race to the short film Arena en el Tiempo – translated as Sand Through Time . Between the speed, tension, and instinct that power the race, and the connection between horse and rider, Abuja amplifies the intensity of the moment through light, and sound, and personal reflections, immortalizing a fleeting instant that hangs suspended in time.

items.text: The Young Ones: Frog For the short film Frog , French-Canadian director and photographer Alex Acy captures the restlessness that rises in a small Quebec town when two teenagers fall in love with the same friend. As the summer unfolds, their friendship and the dynamics of their social circle begin to shift, layered with the recurring thoughts and rambled fears of an unnamed kid – voiced by young Canadian actor Léokim Beaumier-Lépine. Exploring themes of longing, masculinity and forgiveness against the quiet tensions of youth, Acy builds a sense of mood and emotion between hyperreal visuals, music, and voiceover, allowing the film’s separate threads to intertwine and drift apart, evolving in response to each other. “Having this second layer of interpretation responding to the main story is something that has intrigued me for the longest time. I wanted the story to be a conduit for the music and the voiceover instead of the other way around.” Working on the score over two months with producer Charles Mador, Acy developed the story as a conduit for the music and the voiceover instead of the other way around, reversing traditional process while enabling the film’s structure to mirror the formlessness of his characters’ daily existence.

items.text: Diaries: Fishing Lessons For the short film Fishing Lessons , New York-based filmmaker Guy Kozak reflects on romantic relationships through angling and the traditions of male bonding, creating an intimate memento to mark his first wedding anniversary. Shooting over one day in Cape Cod – where his wife grew up and where they were married the previous year – Kozak cast his stepfather-in-law Nat, and his closest friends, Bo & Bill, to deliver their advice on love, life, and fishing, captured against the stillness of the coastal landscape. The fishermen are my stepfather-in-law, and his good friends. I wanted to capture their reflections on life and love, as well as the landscape itself, creating a souvenir that I might look back on as I move forward in my own life and relationship. - Guy Kozak Working with five rolls of expired 16mm film, Kozak embraces the unpredictability and warping of an imperfect medium, while mirroring the uncertainties of both fishing and human connection. Drawing inspiration from the poetic documentary-style of U.S. filmmaker Les Blank, Kozak frames the fishing tradition as a shared space for peace and reflection, highlighting the intimacy, sentimentality and gentleness often missing from portrayals of masculinity.

items.text: Straight Circle Watch the exclusive trailer for filmmaker and prolific music video director Oscar Hudson’s anti-war satire, Straight Circle – premiered at the Venice International Film Festival's 2026 Critics' Week, and awarded winner of its Grand Prize. Set on opposite sides of a remote desert border, Hudson’s debut feature film follows two enemy soldiers, played by Elliott and Luke Tittensor, who slowly lose sight of their identities, and which side they’re fighting for. I have had a long standing fascination with the nationalist identity and I feel like the place where that overlaps with self serious military pomposity is extremely fertile ground for comedy. What begins as a stark, absurdist war story gradually becomes a darkly comic meditation on borders, nationalism, masculinity and the machinery of conflict, descending into an hallucinatory nightmare that grapples with identity, blurring the line between friend and foe. The film is very much about identity and casting the two leads in the way we did brings a strange and enriching meta dimension to the relationship between the two main characters. I allowed the leads to decide between themselves which characters they’d like to play – and then switched them around after casting them. - Oscar Hudson

items.text: Muscle Memory For the short documentary Muscle Memory , director Mikayla Jean Miller follows a community of young Muay Thai boxers in Kharkiv, Ukraine, exploring childhood, connection, bodily wisdom, and growing up just 20km from the frontline. Shot on 16mm film by cinematographer Denys Lushchyk, the film observes how ordinary moments and extraordinary circumstances coexist in the children’s lives, where birdsong, trams, traffic, skipping ropes, laughter, boxing gloves striking pads, and air raid sirens become part of the same sonic landscape. I wanted to show their story in a way that felt relatable, while still holding onto a reality most of us don’t have to think about. What struck me most was how each kid responded to the surrounding sounds – familiar sounds, as well as sounds of war that have become an everyday for them. - Mikayla Jean Miller Revealing the nuances of everyday life under war through urban soundscapes and the children’s reflections, Muscle Memory examines how sound and movement shape memory, identity, and relationship to place, when conflict and its unfamiliar sounds merge with the experiences of youth.

items.text: ICP’s Incubator is located on ICP’s ground floor. The space is free and open to the public during café and museum hours. Since 2018, photographer Melissa Ann Pinney has documented Chicago Public School students as part of an artist residency. As the students began to invite her into their world, the project became a document of identity, community and urgent social issues. Pinney’s thoughtful portraits of young people navigating the transformations of adolescence contain all of the triumph, grief, humor, and tenderness of growing up. About The ArtistMelissa Ann Pinney’s work first garnered attention in the Museum of Modern Art’s major 1991 exhibition, Pleasures and Terrors of Domestic Comfort. Her studies of the social lives and emerging identities of American adolescents have earned her many awards, including a Guggenheim Fellowship, three Illinois Arts Council Fellowship Awards, and a National Endowment for the Arts Midwest Regional Fellowship. Pinney was selected for three documentary projects that were exhibited, published, and archived in Chicago: Changing Chicago (1987), City 2000, and most recently, her work in the Chicago Public Schools. Pinney’s first monograph, Regarding Emma: Photographs of American Women and Girls (2003) was followed by Girl Ascending (2010), TWO (2015), and In Their Own Light: Photographs from Chicago Public Schools (2023).Recent exhibitions include The Outwin 2022: American Portraiture Today, at the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery, Go Down Moses at the Museum of Contemporary Photography Chicago (2019), A History of Photography, at the George Eastman Museum (2019 and 2023), Girl Transcendent at the Schneider International Gallery, Maui (2018), Photographs from the Collection, at the Art Institute of Chicago (2018), American Photographs, 1845 to Now, at the Amon Carter Museum of American Art (2017); The Gender Show, at the Fundación Canal, Madrid, Spain (2016), and Girls on the Verge: Portraits of Adolescence at the Art Institute of Chicago, 2008.Pinney’s photographs are in the collections of the Art Institute of Chicago, George Eastman Museum, J. Paul Getty Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, Museum of Fine Arts Houston, Museum of Modern Art, International Center of Photography, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and Whitney Museum of American Art, among others. About the ICP Incubator SpaceICP’s Incubator Space is a new exhibition program designed to highlight the work of emerging photographers who are responding in real time to the world around us. ICP will present a rotating selection of projects by imagemakers experimenting with and pushing boundaries around the documentary tradition. ICP’s Incubator Space is curated by Sara Ickow, Associate Director of Exhibitions at ICP.

items.text: In On Rape and Institutional Failure, an exhibition centered on the second chapter of her ongoing project A History of Misogyny, Laia Abril examines different forms of violence against women throughout history.Weaving together images, compiled testimonies, archival materials, select objects, and installations with sound and video, the exhibition investigates how gender-based stereotypes, coupled with worldwide prejudices and misconceptions, have contributed to a systemic rape culture that persists today. By focusing on institutions, Abril aims to avoid narratives of victim-blaming, instead addressing the on-going problem of social accountability that has allowed offenders and enablers alike to avoid justice. On Rape and Institutional Failure was first exhibited in 2020 in the wake of the initial, galvanizing allegations against Harvey Weinstein and other powerful men. While #MeToo has led to few sustained consequences and little systemic change, Abril offers a meaningful opportunity to address the long history of silencing victims and the transgenerational trauma that has developed as a result. Please Note: If you are feeling distressed as you move through Laia Abril: On Rape and Institutional Failure, please use the link here for resources and hotlines. https://uniqode.io/J4pZk3 About Laia Abril:Laia Abril (b. 1986) is a research-based artist working across photography, text, video, and sound, focusing on biopolitics and gender issues. Her work is rooted in a politically engaged, process-driven methodology that employs strategies of forensic aesthetics and counter-narratives, interrogating dominant histories and the politics of representation.Her work has been exhibited in over 25 countries and is held in collections such as Centre Pompidou, Photo Elysée, Fotomuseum Winterthur, MACBA, Reina Sofía, MNAC, and the V&A Museum. She has authored acclaimed books, including The Epilogue, Lobismuller, and the A History of Misogyny series: On Abortion, On Rape, and On Mass Hysteria.She has received the Foam Paul Huf Award (Amsterdam), RPS Hood Medal (London), Aperture Best Book Award (NY/Paris), and Spain’s National Photography Award. Based in Switzerland, she is a senior lecturer at HSLU and is represented by Les Filles du Calvaire in Paris and Set Espai d’Art in Spain. About Curator:Sara Ickow is the Associate Director of Exhibitions at the International Center of Photography, where she has been a curator on exhibitions including Gillian Laub: Family Matters, ICP at 50: From the Collection 1845–2019, To Conjure: New Archives in Recent Photography, and Photobooks USA 2000–25. She is also the Managing Director for Women Photograph and co-editor of the book Women Photograph: What We See. Previously, she worked as Curatorial Assistant and Collections Manager at the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery. Sara holds an MA in Art History from NYU’s Institute of Fine Arts. items.text: I’m So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now reconsiders and expands on the history of Japanese photography through the work twenty-eight intergenerational artists from the 1950s to today. Presented in partnership with Aperture and curated by Pauline Vermare, Lesley A. Martin, and Takeuchi Mariko, the exhibition includes work by Fujioka Aya, Hara Mikiko, Hiromix, Ishikawa Mao, Ishiuchi Miyako, Katayama Mari, Kawauchi Rinko, Komatsu Hiroko, Kon Michiko, Nagashima Yurie, Narahashi Asako, Ninagawa Mika, Nishimura Tamiko, Noguchi Rika, Nomura Sakiko, Okabe Momo, Okanoue Toshiko, Onodera Yuki, Sawada Tomoko, Shiga Lieko, Sugiura Kunié, Suzuki Nozomi, Tawada Yuki, Tokiwa Toyoko, Ushioda Tokuko, Watanabe Hitomi, Yamazawa Eiko and Yanagi Miwa.Spanning photography, installation, photobooks, and printed matter, the exhibition explores the experiences and perspectives of women in Japan through delicate and blunt observations of everyday life, critical reflections on the roles inhabited and reshaped by Japanese women, and approaches that push the boundaries of photography. The exhibition is accompanied by a major publication (Aperture, 2024) that expands upon content of the show through essays, historical material, and a comprehensive bibliography of photobooks made by Japanese women.I'm So Happy You Are Here is an exhibition with a strong international pedigree. Following its debut at Rencontres d’Arles, France (2024), the exhibition has traveled to The Hague (2024), Frankfurt (2025), London (2026), and Tokyo (2026), before arriving at ICP for its first US showing here in New York.Financial Times | Arles: “The highlight” of Rencontres d’Arles.W Magazine | London: “The Japanese Women Who Rewrote Photography’s Rules.”Time Out Tokyo | Tokyo: “The exhibition offers a vital counter-narrative to a photographic canon long dominated by male figures.” About Curators:Lesley A. Martin is executive director of Printed Matter. Most recently, she was the creative director of Aperture, where she served as editor on more than one hundred books on photography, and as founding publisher of The PhotoBook Review. Takeuchi Mariko is a photography critic, curator, and professor at Kyoto University of the Arts. Previously, she served as visiting researcher at the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, and at the National Museum of Art, Osaka. Pauline Vermare is the Phillip and Edith Leonian Curator, Photography, Brooklyn Museum. Previously, she served as the cultural director of Magnum Photos in New York, and curator at the International Center of Photography and the Museum of Modern Art, New York. About Aperture:Aperture is a nonprofit publisher that leads conversations around photography worldwide. From its new home opening this September in New York, Aperture connects global audiences and supports artists through its acclaimed quarterly magazine, books, exhibitions, digital platforms, public programs, limited-edition prints, and awards. Established in 1952 to advance “creative thinking, significantly expressed in words and photographs,” Aperture champions photography’s vital role in nurturing curiosity and encouraging a more just, tolerant society. For more information, visit aperture.org Header image: Kawauchi Rinko, Untitled, 2004; from the series the eyes, the ears. Courtesy the artist and Aperture

items.text: If one thing is clear, film photography is not dead. We see it across genres, from commercial fashion photography to enthusiast communities. So, it’s perhaps not a coincidence that Negative Film Conversion has been one of our most requested features. Last year, we got to it. Now, let’s explore how the solution came to life, how it was designed, what needed to be right, and who we collaborated with to bring it to market. Designing the feature: Capture sets the foundation When scanning and converting film, the earliest decisions in the workflow have a lasting impact. That means the quality of the conversion depends heavily on how the negative is captured. To get the best starting point, the goal is to extract as much information as possible from the film, which means maximizing dynamic range and minimizing digital noise during scanning. A camera-based scanning setup with a stable film carrier helps keep the negative sharp, while an even, consistent light source ensures uniform exposure across the frame. items.text: AI needs no introduction. It’s wildly powerful. It ramped quickly and flooded every corner of our lives, and yes, a few big tech companies behaved like hooligans along the way, which naturally created fear, dread, and the sense that something precious was slipping away. But here’s the hard truth: AI has already been adopted. Every single photographer we’ve spoken to in the past six months, and that’s hundreds of them, is using it. Not as a philosophical debate. Not as an existential threat. Just as a tool to run their business. To build mood boards. To finish images. To keep up. AI is reshaping photography at a pace we haven’t seen since the transition from film to digital. And this is uncomfortable. Profoundly uncomfortable. But if there’s anything we’ve learned from Patrick Fore, we need to “sit with the discomfort.” So now the real question is: What future are we building toward?
